doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: His CD, arrogance mellowed, getting it right
summary: Purdie describes his CD showing ten styles, says he has mellowed, and recalls producers paying overtime to get a take right.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Big band, little band, small band, disco, country, R&B, pop, reggae, Brazilian, Latin. It’s all there. And it took me ten years to do because I got solos from all the friends that I wanted, like Dizzy Gillespie, Grover Washington, Jorge Dalto, Freddie Hubbard, the list goes on and on and on or who’s who in the music business. And I kept tracks that I’ve kept over the course of the years up to a forty piece orchestra. And I’ve even done the vocals on some because I wanted a simple melody. I didn’t want all the curly cues that most vocalists want to do first.
It seems like the young R&B singers I hear really — curly — that’s a good word for it.

They’re curly cues. That’s just plain old curly cues. That’s all it is. So you know it’s just one of those things that happened and I’m pleased. I’m just very pleased that I’ve learned to go along with the program. But I’ve also learned how to be a little mellow with things. I’ve gotten pretty good. Structure-wise and everything else. And people doubt — people look at me when I tell them yeah I’m arrogant. And they say well we know that. I said oh man, you’re going to spoil my whole day I can’t even be arrogant anymore. I’m starting to be like I was thirty, forty years ago. “Purdie, forget it.” I mean that arrogance is out the window. No. It’s just not there anymore. It’s not even about that. I like what I do. I’m

good at what I do and I enjoy what I do. And that’s the arrogance as far as it goes. I know now that everything that I do is not going to be one hundred percent totally the right way necessarily. I’ve got to bend. You’ve got to bend the rules sometimes now.
So I lose a few percents. But it’s okay.
You can live with that now.

I can live with it. I couldn’t forty years ago. It was a problem to me forty years ago. I couldn’t walk out the — I’d be totally upset and then I’ve had producer come, “No, no, no, let’s get it right.” I said, “But the time is up.” “We’ll pay the overtime.” Yeah I’ve had them do that. But then of course it was right. I was right and we came back in and we did it and we made hit records with that half hour overtime that we got that they paid for. But it was nice. It was a learning experience. It’s something that I’ll never ever forget. And there’s no way of trying to give it all to somebody at one time in one sitting. It’s just not there, it’s too much. It’s too much going. And it’s going to take years and years and years to get things out of what really happened and why there’s been a major change and a fluctuation to go back to. The music industry itself is hurting. It’s really hurting. And the big guys did it to themselves.
